Cycles per request stayed the same while instructions per request doubled, for example from spinning or extra work
explain: IPC is a ratio. If time and cycles are unchanged, doubling IPC means twice as many instructions were retired per request: busy-waiting or redundant work. That is why IPC must be read alongside the raw instruction count.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Reading the numbers: generic events, pitfalls and top-down
question: On a cloud VM, `perf stat` prints `<not supported>` for cycles and instructions but shows task-clock and page-faults. Why?
options: The hypervisor does not expose the hardware PMU to this guest, so only software events work
perf is too old to know these events
The program ran too briefly to count any cycles
Those events need the :u modifier
explain: task-clock and page-faults are software events maintained by the kernel. Hardware events need PMU access, which a guest only gets if the hypervisor virtualizes it.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
question: A JVM's 32 GiB heap shows AnonHugePages: 0 kB in smaps. THP enabled is set to madvise and defrag to madvise. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The heap is too large for THP
AnonHugePages only counts hugetlbfs pages
khugepaged has not had time to scan 32 GiB yet
The JVM did not mark the heap with madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE), so THP never applies to it
explain: In madvise mode only regions marked with MADV_HUGEPAGE are eligible, at fault time or for khugepaged. An unmarked heap gets zero THP no matter how long you wait. AnonHugePages counts PMD-mapped anonymous THP, not hugetlbfs, and there is no size limit.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: How Jamba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next stack their layers
question: Why does Nemotron-H place a Mamba-2 layer first and use no RoPE in its attention layers?
options: RoPE is incompatible with grouped-query attention
The first Mamba-2 layer is recurrent and naturally encodes position, so explicit position embeddings are not needed
Attention layers at the start would make the KV cache grow quadratically
Mamba-2 layers require RoPE inputs and must come before attention
explain: Waleffe et al. put a Mamba layer at the start so the hybrid can work without position embeddings, since the recurrence itself depends on order. Their 840M ablation also found the no-RoPE hybrid did better after long-context extension.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: A cross-encoder reranks the fused shortlist
question: Your hybrid pipeline reranks the top 20 fused results. Offline analysis shows many relevant documents sit at fused ranks 25 to 60. Which change addresses this most directly?
options: Increase rerank depth N (and possibly each retriever's window) if latency allows
Switch the cross-encoder to a larger model
Lower RRF's k to 1
Remove the BM25 retriever
explain: A better reranker cannot score documents it never sees. Raising N (and the per-retriever windows feeding fusion) brings them into reach; the cost is one more cross-encoder pass per added candidate.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking
question: In the simple model with s = 1 and b = 0.3, going from N = 8 to N = 16 samples moves the cosine from about 0.91 to about 0.93. What does this suggest?
options: Always use N = 16
Shared bias is the main error, so prompt changes cannot help
Most of the remaining gap is the shared bias, so doubling generation cost buys little
Averaging hurts beyond N = 8
explain: The ceiling is 1 over the square root of 1.09, about 0.96. Past N = 8 the independent noise is already small, so extra samples cost tokens for a small gain. Reducing the shared bias (a clearer instruction, keeping the query in the average) is the better lever.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Rejecting bad matches, warping, and direct ECC alignment
question: A drone photographs a city block twice from slightly different positions. Buildings of different heights stand on flat ground. After a RANSAC homography fit, rooftops still show strong differences while the street aligns perfectly. What is the most likely cause?
options: The RANSAC threshold was too low
Rooftops changed brightness
The homography needs more than 8 parameters, so ECC is required
Parallax: the camera center moved, so points off the ground plane do not follow the plane's homography
explain: A homography is exact only for a single plane or for pure rotation. The fitted H follows the dominant plane (the ground), and taller structures shift differently when the camera translates. ECC with MOTION_HOMOGRAPHY has the same 8-parameter limit. Remedies are a dense 3D or optical flow model, or masking out the off-plane regions.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Why epoll plus read still costs a syscall per I/O
question: Why could a server not just add its data files to epoll to get asynchronous buffered file reads?
options: epoll only supports up to 1024 descriptors
epoll works for files but only with O_DIRECT
epoll reports files as ready but read() on them returns EAGAIN
Regular files are not pollable: epoll_ctl rejects them, and a file read can block on the disk however ready the descriptor looks
explain: Readiness has no meaning for a regular file, and `epoll_ctl` returns `EPERM` for one. A read that misses the page cache must wait for the device, so the only pre-io_uring options were a thread pool or Linux AIO with its `O_DIRECT` restriction.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: One skeleton, three allocators: size classes and caches
question: Why can a size-class allocator answer free(p) without a header word in front of each object?
options: The C standard requires callers to pass the size to free
All objects in one page or span share a size class, so the allocator finds the page's metadata from the address and reads the class there
The allocator scans its free lists until it finds the neighbour of p
Each object stores its size in its last 8 bytes
explain: Segregating by size means size is a property of the container. jemalloc looks up the extent for the address, tcmalloc consults its pagemap radix tree, and mimalloc computes the page from the address. C's free does not take a size (C++ sized delete can pass one as an optimization).

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Why a healthy cluster hides consistency bugs
question: Why does Jepsen insist on talking to the database only through its client API instead of reading each replica's internal state?
options: The promise being tested is about what clients observe, so a violation in the client-visible history is exactly a broken promise
Internal state is too large to copy over SSH quickly
Opaque-box tests run faster because no instrumentation is needed
Most databases encrypt their on-disk state
explain: Consistency models are defined over the operations clients perform and the results they get back. If the client-visible history is impossible under the claimed model, the system broke its promise, whatever the internals look like. Speed and encryption are not the reason.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
question: Why does Elle prefer append-only lists over read-write registers?
options: Lists are cheaper to store than integers
A read of a list reveals the whole sequence of prior versions, so the version order (and ww and rw edges) can be inferred from client observations alone
Registers cannot be read inside transactions
Lists make every transaction commit, so there are no aborts to analyze
explain: A blind register write destroys history: you cannot tell which of two writes came first. A list read like [1, 2, 3] traces every version in order, and unique values recover who wrote each one.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Search strategies and the trial budget
question: Why does OpenTuner run an ensemble of search techniques instead of picking the best one?
options: Because running techniques in parallel reduces measurement noise
Because a technique that is optimal for one kind of configuration landscape can fail on another, so credit is assigned at runtime
Because each technique explores a different part of the space by construction
Because ensembles guarantee the global optimum is found
explain: The paper's argument is that landscapes vary: a hill climber suits a smooth, monotonic space, while a discontinuous one may need evolutionary search. The AUC Bandit meta technique allocates more tests to whichever technique is currently producing new global bests. Nothing about this reduces noise or guarantees optimality.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Scaling across cores: one queue per core, rings and mempools
question: To balance load, a developer lets two threads submit I/O to the same SPDK NVMe queue pair. What happens?
options: SPDK detects it and adds a lock automatically
It works, but throughput halves
The second thread's submissions are rejected with an error
Undefined behavior: queue pairs have no locks or atomics, and SPDK does not enforce single-thread use
explain: SPDK's NVMe docs state that violating the one-thread-per-queue-pair rule is undefined behavior and is not checked, because checking would itself need a lock. Give each thread its own queue pair instead.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Vertical and horizontal fusion
question: Which pair is a horizontal fusion opportunity?
options: GELU applied to the output of a bias add
Updating 300 parameter tensors with the same Adam formula in one launch
A softmax whose output feeds a matmul
A dropout applied after GELU
explain: The 300 parameter updates are independent of one another and run the same code, so batching them into one launch is horizontal. The other three are producer-consumer pairs, which is vertical fusion.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
question: A colleague says distillation is pointless if the student has the same architecture as one member of the ensemble teacher, because that architecture was already trained on the data. Based on the speech result, what is the best reply?
options: They are right: the distilled model can never beat a normally trained model of the same size
Only the ensemble matters, so the student should be deleted
The distilled single model recovered most of the ensemble's improvement, so the same architecture trained on soft targets beats the same architecture trained on labels
Distillation only helps when the student is larger than the teacher
explain: Table 1 of Hinton et al.: same architecture, same data, but trained on ensemble soft targets it reached 60.8% frame accuracy versus 58.9% with hard labels. The training targets, not just the architecture, determine what the network learns.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
question: A born-again network (same architecture as its teacher, trained on the teacher's soft targets plus labels) beats its teacher on CIFAR-100. What does this show?
options: The student copied the teacher's weights exactly
Teachers should always be smaller than students
Distillation's benefit is not only compression: soft targets also improve generalization
Distillation only works when fidelity is perfect
explain: No compression happened, yet the student generalized better. Combined with Stanton et al.'s finding that students often do not match their teachers closely, this shows the soft-target signal acts as a regularizer, not just as a copy mechanism.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
question: Why does KVQuant quantize keys before applying RoPE?
options: RoPE rotates channel pairs by position-dependent angles, so a steady outlier channel becomes inconsistent across tokens
RoPE makes keys larger, which overflows FP16
RoPE is only applied to values
Post-RoPE keys cannot be cached at all
explain: Per-channel quantization relies on each channel having a consistent range across tokens. Position-dependent rotation spreads a large channel's energy into its partner, widening both ranges. The cost is reapplying RoPE after dequantization.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
question: Which system is an example of capacity offloading rather than reuse offloading?
options: LMCache storing chunks in Redis for other engines
SGLang HiCache writing radix-tree nodes to host memory
FlexGen placing part of the attention cache in CPU memory during decoding
vLLM's OffloadingConnector copying finished prompt blocks to pinned memory
explain: FlexGen offloads weights, activations and KV of the running batch to fit a huge model on a small GPU and maximize throughput. The other three save KV so later requests that share the prefix can skip prefill.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
question: In the three-node run, which pair of events is related by happened-before?
options: a3 and c2, because a3 is on A, which started the chain
c1 and c2, because they are on the same node and c1 comes first
a3 and b2, because both happen late in the run
c1 and a2, because c1 is drawn to the left of a2
explain: c1 and c2 are on the same process with c1 first, so rule 1 gives c1 happened before c2. There is no message path from a3 to anything, so a3 is concurrent with b2 and c2. c1 and a2 are concurrent too: being drawn further left is not causality.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty
question: An operator lowers CockroachDB's max offset to 250 ms. Using the 80% rule, at what offset from at least half of the other nodes will a node shut itself down?
options: 250 ms
125 ms
200 ms
400 ms
explain: 0.8 x 250 = 200 ms. 400 ms is the threshold for the 500 ms default. A smaller max offset shrinks uncertainty windows (fewer restarts) but makes spurious self-termination more likely when clocks or networks wobble.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Storage: why token vectors are heavy and how ColBERTv2 shrinks them
question: A 200-token passage is stored with ColBERTv2 at 2 bits per dimension, 128 dimensions. How many bytes does it take, ignoring the inverted list?
options: 7,200 bytes
6,400 bytes
51,200 bytes
800 bytes
explain: Each vector is a 4-byte centroid id plus 128 x 2 bits = 32 bytes of residual, 36 bytes total. 200 x 36 = 7,200. 6,400 forgets the centroid id, 51,200 is float16 (200 x 128 x 2), and 800 counts only the ids.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
question: In latent mode at position t (between <bot> and <eot>), what is the input vector?
options: The embedding of the argmax token of softmax(W h at t-1)
A learned <pause> embedding that is the same at every latent position
The last hidden state h at position t-1, after the final normalization
The average of all previous token embeddings
explain: Coconut feeds h(t-1) directly. Taking the argmax token would be ordinary greedy CoT, and a fixed learned embedding is what pause tokens do. Only the direct feedback lets each latent input depend on the full previous computation.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
question: A B-tree with pages of 128 keys and a model with min_err = -40, max_err = +60 both index the same array. In terms of the final search, which statement is right?
options: The model is worse because its errors can be negative
Both leave a range of about 100 to 128 slots to search; they are the same kind of object
The B-tree is exact and the model is approximate, so only the model needs a final search
The model needs no final search if its average error is small
explain: A page is a position estimate with min error 0 and max error 127. The model's range is 101 slots. Both end with a bounded search. That equivalence is the core observation of the paper: a B-tree already is a model with error bounds.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
question: In Bigtable's design a weak model makes some blocks much larger than the target size tau. What breaks?
options: Lookups return wrong rows
Range scans stop working because the model is not monotonic
Nothing is incorrect; block sizes just become uneven, which can cost some read efficiency
Every lookup must now search neighbouring blocks
explain: Records are assigned to block floor(f(k) / tau) by the model itself, so the predicted block is correct by construction. A monotonic f keeps keys sorted so scans still work. A poor fit only makes block sizes less uniform.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Training: ranking loss plus the FLOPS regularizer
question: After raising lambda_q a lot, MS MARCO MRR@10 drops slightly but queries are much faster. What most likely changed?
options: Document vectors got denser
The vocabulary shrank
The ranking loss switched to L1
Query vectors have fewer non-zeros, so fewer posting lists are traversed
explain: lambda_q only penalizes the query representation. Fewer query terms means fewer posting lists to read, at some cost in matching power.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaRank: weight each pair by what a swap does to NDCG
question: After computing lambdas for a query, a teammate finds the per-document pushes sum to 0.37. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing: sums vary from query to query
The query has more relevant than irrelevant documents
The learning rate is too high
There is a bug: each pair adds equal and opposite pushes, so the total must be 0
explain: Every pair contributes +lambda to one document and -lambda to the other, so the sum over a query is exactly zero (up to rounding).

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
question: In the toy, why did $k_A$ and $k_B$ read back perfectly after the first two writes?
options: Because they were written first
Because the values 4 and 2 are small
Because the keys are unit length and orthogonal, so $k_A^\top k_B = 0$ and nothing leaks
Because S was reset between writes
explain: Reading $Sk_A = 4(k_A^\top k_A) + 2(k_B^\top k_A) = 4\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 0 = 4$. Orthonormal keys make the memory exact; overlap is what causes interference.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
question: Bing selects its judge prompt by agreement with which reference?
options: Labels from typical crowd workers
The judge's own labels from a previous week
Careful feedback from real searchers who had the information need
Click-through rate on the live search page
explain: Thomas et al. use first-party gold labels from searchers who had the need, because third-party labellers (crowd or staff) can systematically misread intent. Agreement with crowd labels would only reproduce the crowd's mistakes.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely
question: Your team's reranker is a fine-tuned copy of the same LLM and prompt used to label your offline test set. Offline NDCG@10 jumps from 0.71 to 0.93. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Ship it: a 0.22 gain is far outside noise
Re-evaluate with labels from humans or a judge independent of the reranker, at least on a sample and on the top competing systems
Report the gain with quadratic-weighted kappa instead
Raise the judge temperature to reduce bias
explain: This is the circular setup Faggioli et al. warned about and Clarke and Dietz demonstrated: scores near the ceiling under the judge's own labels while human-labelled NDCG barely moves. Only an independent reference can tell whether the gain is real.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Pairwise preference, Elo and Bradley-Terry ratings
question: Why did Chatbot Arena move from online Elo to Bradley-Terry?
options: Elo cannot handle more than two models
BT needs fewer votes because it ignores ties
Elo ratings cannot be shown on a 400-point scale
Online Elo depends on vote order and favours recent games; BT fits all votes at once assuming fixed strengths, giving stabler estimates and better intervals
explain: The toy showed it: the same 60 votes gave opposite Elo rankings in different orders. The LMSYS blog cites variability in the online algorithm and describes BT as the maximum likelihood estimate of the underlying Elo model.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Defense in depth: input, prompt, output and grounding layers
question: Your RAG app retrieves customer-uploaded PDFs. Which single layer most directly reduces indirect prompt injection from those PDFs?
options: An output profanity word list
Raising the model's temperature
Masking email addresses in the user message
Marking retrieved text as untrusted data (spotlighting) and screening it before it enters the prompt
explain: The attack rides in on the retrieved content, so the defense must act on that content: label it as data and screen it. Word lists and PII masking on the user message do not touch the PDF channel.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Inside an inference server: one engine step at a time
question: A model runs with tensor parallelism over 4 GPUs. Why can one KV cache manager in the scheduler hand the same block table to all 4 workers?
options: Each worker stores the whole KV cache, so memory is simply replicated 4 times
Every shard processes the same token positions and stores only its own heads' slice, so block ids mean the same thing on every GPU
Workers allocate blocks themselves and report back after every step
Block tables are only used on GPU 0, which forwards keys and values to the others
explain: Tensor parallelism splits heads, not positions. Block 17 holds positions 32 to 47 on every GPU, each GPU keeping the K and V of its own heads there. One mapping therefore serves all workers, which is why vLLM centralizes the manager.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
question: A service promises customers that a started response will never stall mid-stream, even at the cost of throughput. Which TensorRT-LLM capacity policy fits?
options: MAX_UTILIZATION
STATIC_BATCH
GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT
Any of them, since in-flight batching never pauses requests
explain: GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT reserves the blocks each request needs to finish before starting it, so started requests are never paused. MAX_UTILIZATION trades that guarantee for more concurrency. STATIC_BATCH is a legacy mode the docs advise against for production.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Why asking nicely for JSON is not enough
question: A pipeline makes 20 LLM calls per job; each yields usable JSON 98 percent of the time, independently. Roughly what fraction of jobs finish without any bad output?
options: 98 percent
about 80 percent
about 67 percent
about 40 percent
explain: 0.98 to the 20th power is 0.668. Per-call reliability that sounds high compounds quickly across chained calls, which is why format errors matter far more in pipelines than in a chat window.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls
question: Which representation of the city should the LLM output for an index with 40000 distinct city IDs?
options: An enum listing all 40000 city IDs so decoding is constrained
The city as a free string, mapped to a canonical ID by a lookup in code
An integer GeoNames ID, since models memorize popular IDs
Nothing: leave cities in the residual text for the embedding to handle
explain: A huge enum exceeds documented schema limits and costs tokens on every request, and models do not reliably know arbitrary IDs, so an invented ID would look valid. Leaving the city in text turns a hard constraint back into a soft one. Extract the surface string and normalize it deterministically.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Anatomy of one rerank call: tokens in, tokens out, two phases
question: With the course assumptions, a prompt of 2,000 tokens produces 60 output tokens. Roughly how is the call time split?
options: About 250 ms prefill and 885 ms decode, so decode dominates
About 1,000 ms prefill and 135 ms decode, so prefill dominates
Equal, since every token costs the same time
Almost all decode, because prefill is processed token by token too
explain: Prefill: 2,000 / 8,000 s = 250 ms. Decode: 59 steps x 15 ms = 885 ms. Prefill processes the prompt in one parallel step; decode cannot.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Prefix caching, truncation and smaller candidate lists
question: You run pointwise reranking on a self-hosted model with prefix caching enabled, but see no cache hits. Your prompt is: passage, then query, then instruction. What is the fix?
options: Raise the cache size
Lower the temperature
Send the passages in a single batch
Put the instruction first, then the query, then the passage
explain: Prefix caching matches from the first token. With the passage first, every prompt differs immediately. Static instruction, then query, then passage makes the first 120 tokens identical across a query's calls.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pairwise ranking prompting: allpairs, sorting and sliding
question: You rerank N = 20 candidates with PRP-Allpair, asking each pair in both orders. How many LLM calls is that?
explain: There are 20 x 19 / 2 = 190 pairs, and each is asked twice (original and swapped order), so 380 calls. For N = 100 the same formula gives 9,900.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Why sending every prompt to the strongest model wastes money
question: Using RouteLLM's blended prices (GPT-4 24.70, Mixtral 0.24 USD per million tokens), a router sends 30% of traffic to GPT-4. What is the blended cost per million tokens?
options: About 7.41, because only the GPT-4 share costs anything meaningful
About 12.47, the same as a 50/50 mix
About 7.58
About 17.36
explain: 0.3 x 24.70 + 0.7 x 0.24 = 7.41 + 0.168 = 7.58. Ignoring the weak model is a fine approximation here (7.41 is close) but not exact. 12.47 is the 50/50 mix and 17.36 corresponds to 70% strong.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail
question: Your router's training labels come from an LLM judge, and you notice it sends almost every prompt that asks for a list to the strong model. Which fix targets the likely cause?
options: Add trusted labels (golden answers or human votes) and evaluate the router on them, controlling for answer length
Lower alpha so more prompts reach the strong model
Replace the router with a cascade
Use a larger embedding model
explain: If the judge prefers longer, more detailed answers (verbosity bias), the router learns to route on length-related features. Trusted labels and an evaluation that controls for length expose and correct that. Moving alpha only shifts the cut; it does not fix what the router learned.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
question: findHomography returns an H that maps the book cover to the wrong place, with only 6 inliers out of 300 matches. What is the most likely cause?
options: The inlier ratio is so low that 2000 iterations never drew a clean sample, often because matching was too loose or the object is absent
The reprojection threshold is too large
RANSAC always fails for homographies
The homography needs 8 points, not 4
explain: With 2% inliers, a clean 4-point sample has probability 0.02^4 = 1.6e-7 per draw, so 2000 iterations almost never find one, and the best random model wins with a handful of accidental inliers. Tighten the ratio test, check the object is visible, or require a minimum inlier count before trusting H.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping
question: Why does a dequeuer at D6 check `head.ptr == tail.ptr` and, if the queue is non-empty, advance Tail before moving Head?
options: To keep Tail from ever pointing at a dequeued node, so dequeued nodes can be safely reused
Because Head and Tail must always be equal
To save one CAS in enqueue
Because Tail must be moved under a lock
explain: The paper: the dequeue ensures Tail does not point to the dequeued node or any predecessor, which is what lets dequeued nodes be reused. Valois's earlier algorithm let Tail lag behind Head and could not safely free nodes for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Spell: templates from the longest common subsequence
question: The prefix tree holds templates DA and ABC, and the line DAPBC arrives. The paper notes the prefix tree returns DA here rather than ABC. Why is that approximation acceptable in Spell?
options: DA is the correct answer: it is the longest template that is a subsequence of DAPBC
A subsequence match is unique, so DA must be the only candidate
Returning DA is a bug that Spell fixes by always falling back to the exhaustive loop
The walk is greedy from the root, so it takes the first matching path; that is almost always right because parameters sit near the end of a line, and the full loop runs when it finds nothing
explain: The prefix tree guarantees only that it returns some template that is a subsequence, not the longest. Spell accepts the approximation because parameters cluster near the end of log lines, and it measured a 100 percent agreement with the exhaustive loop on a 433,490-record HPC log. When the prefilter finds nothing, fewer than 0.1 percent of lines, the full search runs with a Jaccard screen first.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Why models break past their trained length
question: In the toy head (wavelengths 6.3, 62.8, 628.3, 6,283 tokens; trained on 2,048), which pair sees an out-of-distribution angle first as the prompt grows past 2,048 tokens?
options: Pair 0, because it rotates fastest and accumulates the largest angle
Pair 3, because it never completed a full turn during training
All pairs equally, because every position past 2,048 is new
None, because RoPE only depends on relative distance
explain: Pair 0 reaches huge raw angles but wraps every 6.3 tokens, so every angle on its circle was seen thousands of times. Pair 3 only ever covered 0 to 2.047 rad, so at position 2,100 it is already at 2.1 rad, outside its training range.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
question: Ring Attention with 4 ranks and contiguous chunks shows rank 3 at full utilization and rank 0 mostly idle on a causal model. Which change fixes this without changing the math?
options: Increase the block size c
Assign each rank tokens or chunks spread across the sequence (striped or zigzag)
Switch to bidirectional attention
Reduce the number of KV heads
explain: The imbalance comes from the causal triangle: later query chunks attend to more keys. Striped Attention or Llama 3's chunk i plus chunk 2CP - 1 - i assignment gives every rank the same amount of unmasked work.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Recurrent depth at scale: prelude, core block and coda
question: Using the model card's rule (materialized params = 1.5r + 2 billion), what does running Huginn at r = 16 correspond to, and how many effective layers is that?
options: 26B and 68 layers
24B and 64 layers
26B and 64 layers
50B and 132 layers
explain: 1.5 x 16 + 2 = 26 billion. Effective depth is 2 prelude + 4 x 16 core + 2 coda = 68 layers. 50B and 132 layers is the r = 32 point.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
question: You change r from 8 to 16 but keep lora_alpha = 16. Compared with r = 8 and alpha = 16, what happens to the multiplier alpha/r?
options: It doubles from 1 to 2
It halves from 2 to 1
It stays 2, because PEFT rescales alpha automatically
It becomes alpha divided by the square root of r by default
explain: alpha/r goes from 16/8 = 2 to 16/16 = 1. With the default scaling the multiplier depends on r; only use_rslora=True switches to alpha/sqrt(r). Many recipes set alpha proportional to r (for example alpha = 2r) to keep the multiplier constant.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
question: A SISA system with S = 20 shards batches 60 uniformly random deletion requests before retraining. Roughly what fraction of the shard models must be retrained?
options: About 95%, almost every shard is hit at least once
About 5%, one shard per batch
About 33%, since 60 / 20 = 3 requests per shard on average
100% exactly, because 60 is larger than 20
explain: Each shard escapes all 60 requests with probability (1 - 1/20)^60, about 0.046, so about 95.4% of shards are hit at least once. It is not exactly 100% because some shards can get zero requests by chance. This saturation is why SISA's measured speed-ups shrink as requests pile up.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
question: A lab applies RMU to an open-weight model and publishes near-chance WMDP scores as evidence the model is safe to release. What is the strongest objection?
options: WMDP has too few questions to be meaningful
RMU always destroys general capabilities
With open weights anyone can fine-tune on related data, and RMU did not prevent relearning in the WMDP paper's own fine-tuning experiment
Near-chance scores prove the model was never trained on the data
explain: The WMDP appendix reports that fine-tuning an RMU-unlearned Mistral-7B on the forget corpus recovered performance, and Hu et al. show even benign related data can jog the knowledge back. RMU's stated threat model is a closed model unlearned just before serving, not a public release.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Why one GPU cannot train a 175B model, and the five ways to split it
question: A team has a 1.3B model (about 23 GB of model state at 18 bytes per parameter) that fits on one 80 GB GPU with its activations, and wants to train faster on 64 GPUs. Following the Megatron guidance, what should they try first?
options: TP=8 so every layer is split as finely as possible
Plain data parallelism (DP=64), adding model parallelism only if memory runs out
PP=64 so each GPU holds one or two layers
CP=64 so each GPU holds a sliver of each sequence
explain: The Megatron Core guide says to start with data parallelism and add TP, then PP, only when the model does not fit. Model parallelism adds communication and makes per-GPU matrix multiplies smaller, so it is a cost you pay for memory, not a free speedup.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
question: Two runs of the same model on the same GPUs both report 160 TFLOP/s per GPU. Run A uses full recompute, run B uses selective recompute. Which trains faster in tokens per second?
options: Run A, because full recompute frees memory for larger batches
They are the same, the TFLOP/s are equal
Run B, because fewer of its FLOPs are wasted on recomputation, so more go to useful model FLOPs
It cannot be decided without knowing the vocabulary size
explain: Both execute FLOPs at the same rate, but A spends about a quarter of them redoing the forward pass. B's model FLOPs per second, and so its MFU and tokens per second, are higher. This is exactly the HFU vs MFU distinction.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production
question: A Redis instance reports mem_fragmentation_ratio 2.1, with used_memory 40 MB and RSS 84 MB. What should you do?
options: Probably nothing: 44 MB of absolute overhead is small and includes code and libraries
Enable activedefrag immediately
Restart the instance to reset fragmentation
Lower dirty_decay_ms to 0
explain: The Redis docs warn that a high ratio with only a few megabytes of difference is not an issue: the ratio also counts code, shared libraries and stacks, which dominate a small instance. Check allocator_frag_bytes before acting.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: SeqCst, fences, and when you need one global order
question: Why does `Arc::drop` use Release on every `fetch_sub`, rather than only on the one that reaches zero?
options: Because Release makes the decrement faster on x86
Because no thread knows in advance whether its decrement is the last, and every non-final owner's uses must happen-before the deletion
Because fetch_sub cannot be Relaxed
Because SeqCst is required for reference counts
explain: Whichever thread frees the data needs a happens-before edge from every other owner's last use. Each non-final owner provides that by releasing on its decrement; the final owner acquires (via the fence) before deleting. The Acquire is only needed by the one thread that sees old == 1.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
question: N = 8 threads, K = 2 hazard pointers each, R = 2H. What is the maximum number of retired-but-unfreed nodes, and the minimum freed per scan?
options: 16 and 8
32 and 16
128 and 8
explain: H = N x K = 16, so R = 32. The bound is N x R = 8 x 32 = 256 waiting nodes. Each scan checks 32 nodes and at most 16 can be protected, so it frees at least R minus H = 16.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
question: A model trained on the Market-1501 training identities reaches high accuracy on held-out images of those same people. Why does that not tell you it will work for re-ID on Market-1501's test split?
options: Because the test images are smaller than training images
Because accuracy is not defined for embeddings
Because the test identities are different people, so what matters is whether distances generalize to unseen identities
Because re-ID only uses the gallery, never the query
explain: Re-ID test identities are disjoint from training identities. Closed-set accuracy on known people says little about whether the embedding separates new people. You need a retrieval evaluation on unseen identities.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
question: Your team wants to add k-reciprocal re-ranking to a live system that searches a gallery growing by millions of crops per day. What is the main concern?
options: It needs labeled data to retrain the model
It needs neighbor lists for gallery images too, so its cost grows with the gallery and must be recomputed as it changes
It only improves rank-1, never mAP
It only works with ArcFace features
explain: Re-ranking is unsupervised and needs no retraining, but it computes reciprocal neighbors from the gallery's own top-k lists. That is affordable on a fixed benchmark gallery and costly on a large, changing one.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
question: In a JMH run with forks set to 0, benchmark C is 30% slower when it runs after benchmark D than when it runs alone. What is the right fix?
options: Run each benchmark in its own forked JVM, as JMH does by default
Increase warm-up iterations so the JIT settles
Disable ASLR
Add a Blackhole to benchmark C
explain: C inherits JIT profiles from D in a shared JVM, the effect JMHSample_12_Forking demonstrates. More warm-up in the same JVM keeps the polluted profile. ASLR and Blackholes address layout noise and dead code, which are not the problem here.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
question: You serve a MoE with NVFP4 on B200s to speed up rollout but keep the trainer in BF16 to save engineering time. What do the Miles docs say?
options: Supported; add R3 to cover the drift
Supported only with --use-tis
Supported only on Hopper
Unsupported: NVFP4 rollout needs an NVFP4 trainer forward
explain: The compatibility table allows BF16 training with BF16, FP8 block-wise or MXFP8 rollout, but NVFP4 rollout pairs only with NVFP4 training. The report explains that NVFP4 requires every stage that touches the weights to quantize them.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
question: LRB samples training examples uniformly over objects in the memory window rather than over requests. Why?
options: Sampling requests would be too slow to compute
Sampling requests over-represents popular objects, while the decisions LRB must learn are mostly about rarely requested objects it should evict
GBMs cannot train on duplicate objects
Objects that are never requested again would be sampled too often
explain: Per-request sampling picks a hot object once per request, so the dataset fills with objects that should obviously stay. The good evictions, objects beyond the boundary including those never requested again, would be rare. The paper samples over objects so both kinds are represented.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Low-rank joint compression: cache one latent, rebuild every head
question: In DeepSeek-V3, which tensors does an MLA layer write to the KV cache for each new token?
options: The per-head keys $k^C$ and values $v^C$
The query latent $c^Q$ and the key latent $c^{KV}$
The layer input $h_t$, since everything can be recomputed from it
The key-value latent $c^{KV}$ and the shared RoPE key $k^R$
explain: Only $c^{KV}$ (512) and $k^R$ (64) are cached. Queries are never cached. Caching $h_t$ (7168 wide) would be larger and would force recomputing projections for every past token.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, results
question: A blog says MLA alone cut DeepSeek-V2's KV cache by 93.3% vs MHA. What is wrong with that claim?
options: 93.3% is measured against DeepSeek 67B (a GQA model) for the deployed system, which also quantizes the cache; MLA vs MHA in matched models was 14% to 4% of the MHA cache
Nothing, that is exactly what the paper measured
MLA increases the KV cache
93.3% refers to training cost
explain: The abstract compares V2 to DeepSeek 67B. The matched MHA vs MLA comparison is Table 9: 15.6K vs 110.6K and 34.6K vs 860.2K elements per token.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Thousands of adapters: S-LoRA's unified paging and loading
question: A burst of requests touches 40 rarely used adapters at high rank. In S-LoRA's design, what is the most direct cost?
options: The base model must be reloaded
Requests for those adapters must wait for a merge
Adapter pages take space from the KV cache, reducing how many requests fit in a batch, and each adapter must be fetched from host memory
SGMV can no longer batch rows together
explain: Adapters live in host memory and are fetched on demand into the unified pool. Each active adapter uses pages that the KV cache could have used, so many large ones at once cut the batch size. Nothing is merged, and batching still works.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
question: In the toy, why does d2 (not relevant) outrank d7 (relevant) after fusing all four lists?
options: d2 has a higher cosine similarity
d2 appears in two lists while d7 appears in only one, and RRF sums contributions
RRF gives rank 1 a weight of zero
d7 was removed by deduplication
explain: RRF adds one term per list. d2 gets 1/62 + 1/65 = 0.03151; d7 gets only 1/61 = 0.01639 even though it was ranked first by q2. Agreement beats a single strong vote.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Candidate depth k and the recall ceiling
question: Your RAG search uses BM25 top 100 and a strong cross-encoder. You swap in a cross-encoder twice as large and nDCG@10 barely moves. Stage 1 recall@100 is 0.62. What is the most likely bottleneck?
options: The new cross-encoder is undertrained
The ceiling: 38% of relevant documents never reach the reranker, so stage 1 recall or k must improve
nDCG@10 cannot measure reranker quality
k = 100 is too deep and confuses the reranker
explain: With recall@100 of 0.62, the reranker never sees 38% of relevant documents. Bigger rerankers only reorder the 62% they receive. Raise the ceiling: hybrid first stage, better embeddings, or a larger k if the budget allows.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
question: A 10-token sequence is trained with n = 4 independent future heads. How many loss terms does it contribute (count head i as having 10 - i targets)?
options: 9, because only the next-token head counts
40, because each of 10 positions has 4 targets
36, because 4 x 9
explain: Head 1 has targets for positions 1 to 9, head 2 for positions 1 to 8, and so on: 9 + 8 + 7 + 6 = 30. Positions near the end have fewer valid future tokens, so the count is not simply 10 x 4.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
question: You serve a Gloeckle-style 4-token model with greedy decoding and enable self-speculative decoding with all 4 heads. What happens to the generated text?
options: It becomes more diverse because heads 2 to 4 inject their own choices
It is identical to greedy decoding with head 1; only the number of forward passes drops
It is identical only if every draft is accepted
It degrades slightly, which is the price of a 3x speedup
explain: Every emitted token is one that head 1 would have chosen given the same prefix: drafts are kept only when they match head 1's prediction, and the first mismatch is replaced by head 1's token. Acceptance rate changes speed, never content.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
question: You need to estimate SOAP's optimizer memory for a $4096 \times 4096$ matrix, counting state plus the gradient as the paper does. Which is closest?
options: 33.6M floats, one buffer like Muon
50.3M floats, the same as AdamW
117.4M floats
281 trillion floats, like full-matrix AdaGrad
explain: $2m^2 + 2n^2 + 3mn$ with $m = n = 4096$ is $33.6 + 33.6 + 50.3 \approx 117.4$ million. AdamW uses $3mn = 50.3$M (gradient, first and second moment); Muon uses about $2mn = 33.6$M (gradient and one momentum buffer).

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: The muP rules, layer by layer
question: Your model ties the input embedding and output unembedding weights. Which muP formulation from the paper fits best?
options: Table 3, because it is the main table
Neither; muP cannot be used with tied embeddings
Table 8, which gives input and output weights the same init and LR scaling and puts a 1/fan_in multiplier on the logits
SP with a smaller global learning rate
explain: Table 3 initializes output weights with variance $1/\text{fan\_in}^2$ but input weights with $1/\text{fan\_in}$, which conflicts if they are the same tensor. Table 8 is an equivalent formulation where all vector-like parameters share one rule and the width factor moves into a forward multiplier, so tying works. `MuSharedReadout` implements this.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
question: In the cost model, sleeping costs C = 5 units and you spin for a budget B = 5 before sleeping. The lock turns out to be held for W = 3 units. What do you pay?
options: 5 units, because you always sleep eventually
10 units
8 units
3 units: the lock frees up during the spin
explain: W = 3 is within the budget, so you spin 3 units, take the lock, and never sleep. That equals the best in hindsight, min(3, 5) = 3.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
question: A table has 1 row that has been updated 3 times since it was inserted, and no VACUUM has run. How many tuples for that row are on disk?
explain: The insert created one tuple and each of the 3 updates wrote another, so there are 4 tuples. Only the newest has xmax = 0; the other 3 wait for VACUUM.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
question: An UPDATE changes only a non-indexed `last_seen` column, and the page has free space. What does HOT save compared with a normal update?
options: It avoids writing a new tuple version at all
It avoids new index entries, and lets old versions be pruned without VACUUM
It skips writing to the WAL
It makes the update visible to concurrent snapshots
explain: HOT still writes a new tuple version (MVCC requires it), but on the same page and without new index entries. Intermediate versions can be pruned during normal page access.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Scoring whole sequences: transitions and Viterbi by hand
question: Your BIO tagger has no CRF and sometimes emits `O I-ORG I-ORG`. Which response still leaves that sequence possible?
options: Add a CRF layer so the training loss sees label transitions and Viterbi cannot take an invalid one
Switch to BIOES so the output layer has 17 labels instead of 9
Keep the independent softmax but mask out transitions the scheme forbids during decoding
Decode with a beam that only extends well-formed BIO prefixes
explain: BIOES makes the tag set larger and the end of a span explicit, but with independent per-token softmaxes nothing rules out an impossible sequence: you can still emit O then I-ORG, now with 17 labels. The other three all make the invalid path unreachable, either in the loss or in the decoder.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
question: With NSA's settings ($d=16$, $n=16$, $l'=64$, $w=512$), which term of the per-query key count dominates at a 1M-token context?
options: The compressed tokens, about $t/d \approx 65{,}500$
The selected tokens, $nl' = 1024$
The window, $w = 512$
All three are equal
explain: Selection and window are fixed sizes. Compression grows linearly with $t$ at rate $1/d$, so at long context it dominates: about 65,534 of roughly 67,070 keys at 1,048,576 tokens.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
question: Why does aHash squash the image to 8x8 without keeping the aspect ratio?
options: So that the hash fits in a 64-bit integer, which is the only reason
Because grayscale conversion only works on square images
To keep high-frequency detail that distinguishes near copies
So that a resized or stretched copy reduces to nearly the same 64 pixels and therefore the same bits
explain: The shrink is what makes the hash scale-invariant: every size and aspect ratio of the same picture is crushed to the same 8x8 grid. It also discards high frequencies on purpose, the opposite of the last option.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
question: Why does PDQ use 256 bits where pHash uses 64?
options: 256-bit integers are faster to XOR
More bits keep unrelated images far apart even in web-scale collections, where a 64-bit hash with a useful threshold yields many chance matches
The DCT requires 256 outputs
To store the image's color histogram
explain: With 64 bits and threshold 10, uniform random hashes already give about 10 chance candidates per query in a billion images. With 256 bits and threshold 31, the random-collision rate is astronomically small; the PDQ authors call 256 bits appropriate for web scale.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Colocated vs non-colocated generation, and how weights are refit
question: A single node has 8 GPUs. You set colocated.enabled: false and colocated.resources.gpus_per_node: 8. What happens?
options: Training and generation each get 8 GPUs
Setup fails because training would get 8 - 8 = 0 GPUs
NeMo RL falls back to colocated mode
Generation gets 4 and training gets 4
explain: On one node, training gets cluster.gpus_per_node minus the inference GPUs. The setup asserts that the result is greater than 0, so this config is rejected.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
question: You call `mbind(p, len, MPOL_INTERLEAVE, ...)` with flags 0 on a range that the program already filled with data from one thread on node 0. What changes?
options: Existing pages are rebalanced across both nodes immediately
Nothing for existing pages; only pages allocated later in the range are interleaved
The call fails because the range is already populated
explain: Policies apply at allocation time. Without MPOL_MF_MOVE the existing pages stay on node 0. With MPOL_MF_MOVE the kernel tries to migrate them, though pages already on a listed node are not reshuffled into an interleave.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: The flash translation layer: a log plus a map
question: A block-mapped FTL stores logical pages 2000 to 2003 in one 4-page physical block. The host overwrites only 2002. How many pages must be programmed?
explain: With one pointer per block, the block's pages must stay together in order. The FTL reads 2000, 2001 and 2003, then writes all four (with the new 2002) into a fresh block. With real 64-page blocks that is 64 programs for one host page.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
question: A drive delivers 500,000 random 4 KB reads per second at 100 us average latency. How many reads must the application keep outstanding to reach that rate?
explain: Little's law: outstanding = throughput x latency = 500,000 x 0.0001 s = 50. With fewer in flight, the drive's dies sit idle and throughput drops in proportion.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
question: A store counts visitors by summing per-frame person detections over an hour of 30 fps video. What is the main problem?
options: NMS removes too many people
The density map is not normalized
COCO AP is too low
Each person is counted once per frame they are visible, so the total measures person-frames, not people
explain: A person visible for 10 seconds appears in about 300 frames and adds about 300 to the sum. Tracking links those detections into one identity, and counting entries (line or region crossings) gives a count of people.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Keeping object storage off the hot read path
question: A service runs at a 99% cache hit rate. During a deploy, all nodes restart with empty caches. What do users see, and what is the best mitigation?
options: Nothing, S3 is fast enough
Writes fail until caches refill
A latency spike toward S3 GET latency until caches warm; pre-warm hot data and roll restarts so routing keeps most caches warm
Stale reads, because caches were cleared
explain: With h near 0 every read is a miss, so latency jumps from about 2.5 ms toward 150 ms in our model. Data is never stale or lost, since S3 holds it. Rolling restarts and pre-warming the hottest objects keep the hit rate high while nodes come back.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
question: The SLO is 99.9 percent over 30 days. For one hour the error ratio sits at 1.0 percent. How much of the monthly error budget does that hour spend?
options: 0.14 percent
10 percent, because 1 percent is ten times the allowance
1.39 percent
100 percent, since the error ratio exceeded the SLO
explain: The burn rate is 0.01 / 0.001 = 10, and budget spent is burn rate times window over period: 10 x 1/720 = 1.39 percent, about 36 seconds of the 43.2-minute monthly budget. The 10 percent answer confuses the burn rate with the fraction spent, which would be true only if the hour were the whole window.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut
question: In LayoutLM's input, why are the coordinates scaled to integers between 0 and 1000?
options: To compress the page image
Because BERT's vocabulary has 1000 tokens
So the same position means the same relative place on any page size, and the integer can index an embedding table
To make the boxes rotation invariant
explain: The paper scales coordinates to a virtual 0 to 1,000 range because page sizes vary. The integer values are looked up in learned X and Y tables, so they must be bounded integers.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
question: Configure succeeds, compile succeeds, then the link of `app` fails with: undefined reference to `tensor_new`, called from add.o in libops.a. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add target_link_libraries(ops PUBLIC core) (or PRIVATE) so core is linked after ops
Add core's include directory to app
Rebuild with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
Delete the build directory, since the cache is stale
explain: The symbol is referenced from inside libops but defined in libcore. Without a declared ops to core edge, nothing guarantees core is searched after ops. Include paths affect compiling, not linking, and the cache is not involved.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Running exactly the tests that matter with pytest
question: You are fixing one failing test among 4,000 and want each rerun to execute only the tests that failed last time. Which command?
options: `pytest --ff`
`pytest -x`
`pytest --lf`
`pytest -k failed`
explain: `--lf` (last failed) reruns only the recorded failures. `--ff` runs failures first but then the whole suite. `-x` still starts from the beginning and stops at the first failure. `-k failed` matches test names containing the word failed, which has nothing to do with results.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Answering review comments as the author
question: A reviewer writes: "I can't tell what this regex is matching." Which response best follows the guidance in this lesson?
options: Reply in the thread with a full explanation of the regex
Resolve the conversation, since it is a question and not a change request
Ask the reviewer to read the regex documentation
Split the regex into named parts or add a comment explaining what it matches, then reply pointing to it
explain: If the reviewer cannot follow the code, future readers will not either. Clarifying the code (or adding a comment when it cannot be simpler) fixes the problem for everyone. A thread reply only helps this one reviewer, and silently resolving leaves the question unanswered.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
question: An org keeps CONTRIBUTING.md only in its public `.github` repository. Repo `org/tool` has `docs/CONTRIBUTING.md`. Which file does GitHub link when you open a PR on `org/tool`?
options: `docs/CONTRIBUTING.md`, because the repository's own file wins over the account default
The org-wide file, because the .github repository always takes precedence
Neither: the file must be in the repository root to be linked
Both are shown, merged into one page
explain: The account-level `.github` repository is a fallback used only when the repository has no file of that type. The repository's own file in `.github/`, root, or `docs/` wins, checked in that order.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
question: You cloned your fork and ran `git fetch upstream`, but it fails with "'upstream' does not appear to be a git repository". What is the most likely cause?
options: Your fork is out of date with the original repository
You never ran `git remote add upstream URL`, so the name is unknown
You need to push to origin before you can fetch
The original repository has a different default branch name
explain: Cloning creates only the `origin` remote. `upstream` is just a name you add yourself with `git remote add`; until then Git does not know what it refers to. Being out of date or having a different default branch does not make the remote name unknown.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
question: A project's CI says "DCO check failed: commit 9782e95 has no Signed-off-by". The other two commits are signed off. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Add a comment on the PR saying you agree to the DCO
Run `git commit -S` to sign the latest commit with GPG
Run `git rebase --signoff upstream/main`, then force-push with a lease
Close the PR and open a new one with a different branch name
explain: The trailer must be in the commit message itself, so the commit has to be rewritten. `git rebase --signoff` adds it to every replayed commit (in our test, commits that already ended with the same trailer did not get a second copy), then you update the PR with a guarded force-push. `-S` is a cryptographic signature, not a sign-off.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
question: Your employer signed Google's corporate CLA, yet the CLA check on your PR fails. What is the most likely cause?
options: Corporate CLAs only cover Google employees
Your commit email is not in the employer's authorized contributor group or not linked to your GitHub account
The project uses inbound=outbound, so CLAs are ignored
You must also assign copyright to Google
explain: Google maps contributions to a CCLA through the email addresses in the organization's group, and asks contributors to use that address in git and on GitHub. The CLA grants a license; you keep ownership.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? t-tests, U tests and p-values
question: Your benchmark's noise CV drops from 2% to 1% after CPU pinning. Roughly how does the number of runs needed to detect the same change scale?
options: It halves
It stays the same
It drops to about a quarter
It doubles
explain: Runs needed scale with the square of noise over effect: n is about 2 (t CV / delta) squared. Halving CV cuts n by about 4, from 32 to 9 runs per side for a 1% change in the worked model.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: git blame: who last changed a line, and seeing past noise
question: A commit moved a 30-line function from the top of a file to the bottom, unchanged, past another function. Plain blame credits the moved lines to the move commit. Which option is designed for this?
options: -w
-M
--first-parent
-e
explain: -M detects lines moved or copied within a file and blames them on the parent. -w only ignores whitespace differences, --first-parent changes how merges are walked, and -e shows email addresses instead of names.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: git bisect: finding the commit that introduced the bug
question: Your bisect test is a small C program that calls `exit(-1)` when the bug is present. What happens?
options: Git treats it as bad, because any non-zero code means bad
Git treats it as a skip, like 125
The exit status becomes 255, which is outside 0 to 127, so git aborts the bisect
explain: Exit statuses are truncated to 8 bits, so exit(-1) leaves 255. The git docs say any code other than 0, 125 or 1 to 127 aborts bisect run. Use exit 1 for bad.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: A title and description that explain why
question: A project uses squash merging, and GitHub's default squash message can include the PR title and description. You titled the PR `wip` and left the body empty. What is the lasting cost?
options: The main branch can get a commit titled `wip` with no explanation, which future readers of git log and git blame will see
None: squash merging discards the PR title
GitHub blocks squash merges of PRs with short titles
Only the review is slowed; history is unaffected
explain: GitHub's docs say the default squash commit message can include the PR title and description. A maintainer can edit it, but a vague title often ends up as the permanent commit summary.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks
question: Block size 16. Request X has a 100-token prompt. Request Y shares X's first 40 tokens, then differs. With X's blocks still cached, how many of Y's prompt tokens are reused?
options: 0, because the prompts differ
explain: Only full blocks that match from the start are reused. Tokens 0 to 15 and 16 to 31 form two matching full blocks; the third block (32 to 47) contains differing tokens, so its hash differs. 2 x 16 = 32 tokens are reused; the other 8 shared tokens are recomputed.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
question: A thread profile shows `hash_lookup` as a 5% tower under `parse` and a 25% tower under `index`, and nowhere else. What share of samples include hash_lookup?
options: 25%, take the widest tower
15%, the average
You cannot tell without the call count
explain: The same function under different callers appears as separate towers. Since no stack can contain both (they are disjoint paths here), the shares add: 5% + 25% = 30%, which is what the search feature reports.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Flushes, fences and the order things become durable
question: A record has two 8-byte fields, version and value, in different cache lines, and you update both in place with two ordinary stores, then persist both. A crash happens before the persist completes. How many of the 4 combinations of old and new fields can appear after reboot?
options: Only 2: all old or all new
3: the hardware never persists value before version
1: the persist call makes the update atomic
4, two of which are torn mixes of old and new
explain: Each 8-byte field is failure-atomic on its own, but together they are 16 bytes: old/old, new/new, old/new and new/old are all reachable, so 2 of the 4 are torn. pmem_persist is explicitly not atomic. You need an out-of-place copy or a log.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
question: What is `sizeof(struct T)` for `struct T { int i; char c; };` on x86-64?
explain: i is at 0 (4 bytes), c at 4, so the data ends at 5. The struct alignment is 4 (from int), so the size rounds up to 8. The 3 bytes of tail padding keep `i` aligned in every element of a `struct T` array.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
question: A COCO ground-truth person has the left wrist marked with v = 1. What does that mean?
options: The annotator placed the wrist, but it is hidden (for example behind the torso)
The wrist was not annotated at all, so it is ignored
The wrist is visible and annotated
The wrist was predicted by a model, not a person
explain: v = 0 means not labeled, v = 1 labeled but not visible, v = 2 labeled and visible. Occluded joints still get a position, so a model is expected to guess where a hidden wrist is.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps
question: Why can BlazePose drop its heatmap branch at inference and still benefit from it?
options: The heatmap and offset losses supervise shared features during training, and the regression head uses those features at inference
Heatmaps were only used to visualize results
The heatmaps are cached from the first frame
MediaPipe computes heatmaps on the GPU separately
explain: The paper uses heatmap and offset losses only in training, then removes those output layers. They act as extra supervision that shapes the shared features, while the cheap regression head produces the coordinates at run time.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Query planners: choosing a strategy by selectivity
question: Your pgvector query with WHERE category_id = 123 (one of 5 categories, about 20% of rows) returns too few rows. Which fix targets the root cause most directly?
options: Lower hnsw.ef_search to 10
Drop the HNSW index
Increase LIMIT
Enable hnsw.iterative_scan or build a partial HNSW index WHERE category_id = 123
explain: The shortfall comes from post-filtering a fixed candidate list. Iterative scans keep fetching until enough rows pass; with only a few distinct values, a partial index per value makes every candidate a match. Lowering ef_search makes it worse, and LIMIT does not change how many candidates are scanned.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Software prefetch: distance, hints and the kernel's lesson
question: Spot the problem: `for (p = head; p; p = p->next) { __builtin_prefetch(p->next); work(p); }` on a list of 3 nodes that is walked millions of times.
options: It can crash when p->next is NULL
The prefetch needs locality 0 to be legal
Nothing: the hardware ignores prefetches of NULL at no cost
Distance 1 is too short to hide a miss behind `work`, and on every walk the last prefetch targets NULL, which Intel says can cause long delays
explain: This is the kernel's list pattern. A prefetch never faults, so there is no crash, but one hop ahead hides little latency on a short list, and the NULL prefetch at the end of every walk was measured at about 20 cycles. The kernel removed these prefetches.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL
question: With a PRM, beam search beats best-of-N on medium-hard MATH problems (levels 3 and 4) but loses on easy ones as the budget grows. What explains the easy-problem loss?
options: On easy problems the PRM is mostly right already, so stronger search mainly exploits its spurious preferences
Beam search uses fewer samples than best-of-N at the same budget
Easy problems have fewer steps, so the PRM cannot score them
Weighted voting is disabled in beam search
explain: Snell et al. interpret it this way: on easy questions the verifier is mostly correct, so extra optimization amplifies its errors (e.g. repetitive or overly short solutions). On harder questions the base model rarely samples the right path, so guidance helps.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a context switch, step by step
question: Two threads of the same process alternate on one CPU. Compared with two separate processes alternating, which step does the kernel skip?
options: Saving and restoring the general-purpose registers
Switching kernel stacks
Loading a new page table root (CR3 on x86) and the TLB work that comes with it
Running the scheduler to pick the next task
explain: Each thread still has its own registers and kernel stack, so those are always swapped, and the scheduler always runs. Only the address space is shared, so switch_mm finds the same mm and returns without touching CR3.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Why billion-vector indexes need compressed codes
question: Why can't we just run k-means with 2^64 centroids to get 64-bit codes directly?
options: k-means only works in two dimensions
64-bit integers overflow on most CPUs
Training needs several times 2^64 samples and the centroids alone could not be stored
The resulting codes would be longer than 64 bits
explain: The PQ paper's argument: learning needs many more samples than centroids, the assignment cost scales with k, and storing D x 2^64 floats is impossible. Product quantization gets the same number of reproduction values from m small codebooks.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
question: Which ingredient, if missing, makes automatic prompt optimization impossible rather than just slower?
options: A large proposer model
Thousands of training examples
A metric that can score an output on an example
Access to the target model's gradients
explain: Search needs a way to compare candidates. Small dev sets work (OPRO used 3.5% of the GSM8K training set) and APE, OPRO and DSPy are all black-box, so no gradients are needed. Without a metric there is nothing to maximize.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Managed prompt optimizers and a practical workflow
question: You move a production prompt that was optimized with DSPy for one model to a different model. Based on this course, what should you do?
options: Nothing: compiled prompts are model-independent
Only re-run the test set, never the optimizer
Re-compile against the new model with the same metric and splits, then compare both on the test set
Delete all demos, since demos never transfer
explain: Lesson 1 showed the best wording is model-specific: on GSM8K the APE trigger won with InstructGPT and lost by 13 points with PaLM 2-L. Keeping the metric and splits fixed makes the re-optimized prompt directly comparable with the old one.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
question: Why does RFdiffusion run AlphaFold2 on the single designed sequence, with no multiple sequence alignment?
options: A designed sequence has no natural homologues, so an MSA would either be empty or misleading; single-sequence prediction is also the harder, more honest test
Because AF2 is faster without an MSA and the pipeline needs throughput
Because MSAs are only used for membrane proteins
Because the sequence is already known to be correct, so extra evidence would bias the result
explain: A de novo design is not a member of any natural protein family, so there is nothing meaningful to align it to. Running single-sequence prediction also means the model must fold the design from its own learned physics, which is a stricter test than letting it copy a homologue.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
question: A rule `personal computer => pc` is used at search time. A user types `personal computer`; a document contains only `personal computer`, never `pc`. What happens?
options: It matches, because explicit rules keep both sides
It does not match through the synonym: the query is rewritten to pc, and the document was indexed without that rule
It matches only with expand: false
The analyzer rejects the rule because multi-word left sides are invalid
explain: An explicit rule replaces the left side with the right side. Applied only at search time, the query becomes pc, which this document does not contain. Use an equivalent rule (personal computer, pc) or include the original on the right side if both should match.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
question: In the toy, why did concatenating all three turns still rank the RAID disk document first?
options: Because BM25 ignores words from earlier turns
Because the disk document is the longest
Because concatenation removes the word raft
Because the concatenated query still contains happens and fails, which together match only the disk document
explain: Concatenation keeps every word of the current turn. happens appears only in d3, so it has a high IDF, and d3 matches both happens and fails. Adding raft and leader helps d2 but not enough to overtake it.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Paying for it: latency, cost and when not to rewrite
question: Your rewriter makes 30% of first-turn queries slightly worse and adds 0.5 s to every request. Which change most directly addresses both problems?
options: Use a larger rewriter model
Generate 5 rewrites instead of 1
Concatenate the history instead of rewriting
Skip rewriting when the turn is already standalone (first turn, no unresolved references) and keep the original query otherwise as a fallback
explain: Gating removes the call where it adds no value (cutting latency) and avoids the drift it introduces on queries that were already fine. A larger model costs more time; more rewrites multiply drift; concatenation reintroduces stale-topic problems.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound
question: Why can the error bound replace the usual 'rerank the top R candidates' hyperparameter?
